en: The Verses of Exhortation to the King by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang.
These verses were composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna as a letter in poetic form, sent to his relative in South India.
One fascicle of the *Suhṛllekha* (Letter to a Friend), King of the Śātavāhana Dynasty.

This work was previously translated and included in the Tripitaka during the time of the Divine Land (China), yet as many people have not seen it, its exquisite phrasing has consequently remained largely unknown.
For this reason, I have further revised the original text, hoping that it may circulate without obstruction.
The Śramaṇa Yijing first arrived at the kingdom of Tāmraliptī in Eastern India and translated it there.
Because sentient beings have their minds shrouded by ignorance, Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva gave rise to compassion to enlighten and liberate them;
as a great master, he sent a letter to the king, entrusting him to practice and study.
This single verse was composed by a later author to indicate the essential meaning of the original work:
"I, the Virtuous One, proclaim this teaching of Suchness; I have composed it to generate merit and affection.
The truly virtuous should listen with careful attention; this verse is named 'The Noble Gāthā'."
Whichever wood or other material is used to carve an image of the Buddha, all who possess wisdom shall offer it worship;
even if my poem is not skillfully crafted, do not treat it with contempt, for it is spoken in accordance with the True Dharma.
Although the King had previously understood the teaching of suchness, hearing the Buddha’s words further increased his resolute faith;
like the radiance of moonlight upon a plastered wall, how could it not be brilliant and even more exquisite?
The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, Generosity, morality, and the devas—
These clusters of merit, the Buddha taught, Should be constantly recollected.
Regarding the ten paths of wholesome action, One should always cultivate them through body, speech, and mind.
Abstaining from all intoxicants, one also leads a pure livelihood.

Knowing that the essence of wealth is not firm, one gives according to the Dharma to bhikṣus, the poor, the lowly, and those of twice-born status; thus, they shall become one’s kinsmen in future lives.
All virtues abide in the precepts, Just as the earth nurtures all things.
Do not be negligent, emaciated, or distracted by worldly desires; The Buddha taught that one should always practice them.
Generosity, morality, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration— Their wisdom is beyond measure.
This is what one who can reach [the goal] should cultivate, to cross the ocean of existence and become a Buddha.
If one filially supports one’s parents, that household will have a Brahmā King;
it will manifestly attract a good reputation, and in future lives one will be born in heaven.
Abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech; Refraining from indulgence in food, attachment to high beds,
And all intoxicants, dancing, singing, Flowers, perfumes, and ointments—
if a man or woman can accomplish These eight branches of the noble precepts, [they shall attain the fruits of the holy life].
Above the six heavens of the desire realm, one shall be born through the merit of long-term purification.
Greed, flattery, deception, craving, and indolence; pride, lust, anger, and the influence of family lineage;
as well as much learning, youth, and vanity—regard all these together as enemies and thieves.
It is said that non-arising results from diligence, while death exists because of negligence;
diligence can cause wholesome dharmas to grow, so you should practice heedfulness.
If one was previously negligent but later reforms to practice with diligence, [one will attain the goal].
Just as when clouds and mists are cleared away,
one beholds the bright moon on a fine night; so too, Sundarananda,
Aṅgulimāla, and Daśagrīva— those who were formerly evil— all became virtuous.
Exert yourself with peerless patience; do not allow the power of anger to prevail.
You shall ultimately attain the stage of Non-returning, for the Buddha has testified that hatred can be eliminated.
Even if others strike or revile me, or deceive, insult, and rob me of my wealth—
Harboring resentment invites enmity and strife; by relinquishing resentment, one sleeps in peace and happiness.
Just as with water, earth, and stone, the human mind is entirely like them;
those who give rise to afflictions are like the former, while those who cherish the Dharma are like the latter.

The Buddha has spoken of three kinds of speech: those that are beautiful yet false, those that are true yet harsh, and those that are both true and pleasant. One should discard the latter and practice the former.
That which is clear now will be clear later; that which is dark now will remain dark later.
Some are bright now but dark later; some are dark now but bright later.
Regarding these four types of people, O King, you should rely upon the first.
Some are born as if already ripe; others are ripe as if still raw.
Some are ripe as if ripe, while others are raw as if raw;
within the *āmra* fruit there are such distinctions.
Humans likewise possess these four types, which are difficult to discern—this the King should know.
Do not gaze upon the wives of others; if you must look, view them as a mother or a daughter, or as a sister according to their age. Should thoughts of desire arise, contemplate impurity.
Just as one would protect the life of a son in the womb, so should one guard against a restless mind.
The beastly medicine, the sword, resentment, and fire—let not sensual pleasures invade you.
Because desire brings about what is disadvantageous, it is like the fruit of a poisonous tree;
the Buddha taught that it should be abandoned, for it is the firm shackles of birth and death.
Deceitful and ever-shaking the sensory realms, One who can subdue these six consciousnesses, Wielding the staff to sweep away all enemies, Is granted the title of the ultimate hero.
The nine gates emit foul odors, a chamber of manifold impurities; This wretched body, difficult to fill, is bound by thin skin.
Behold the young woman, stripped of her finery and makeup; Her disfigured body is beyond description.
When leprosy-infesting worms have burrowed through, the pain is such that she seeks relief by the fire;
Yet even there she finds no respite from her suffering— Such is the same case for those who indulge in desire.
To know the truly supreme principle, one should attend to and contemplate all phenomena;
only this virtue should be cultivated, for there is no other dharma to be relied upon.
Even if a person possesses noble lineage, a beautiful appearance, and great learning—
One who lacks wisdom and violates the precepts— how can such a person be worthy of esteem?
If a person has no noble lineage, an ugly appearance, and little learning,
yet possesses wisdom and guards the precepts, all people should offer them support.
Gain and loss, suffering and pleasure, fame and insignificance, praise and blame—
having thoroughly understood these eight worldly dharmas, unify the mind and depart from this realm.
For the twice-born heavenly seeker, parents, wife, and children [are but attachments].
Do not commit sins on this account; the fruits of hell cannot be shared with others.
If you perform various sinful deeds, they are no different from being wounded by a blade;
yet it is only when the moment of death arrives that the full retribution of evil karma is revealed.
Faith, virtue, generosity, purity, learning, Shame, dread of blame, and right wisdom— These are the seven treasures taught by the Muni;
They are truly shared possessions, not empty words.
Gambling, idle pleasures, and noisy distractions, Laziness, and intimacy with evil friends— These are the things one should firmly resolve to avoid.
Drinking alcohol at improper times incurs six faults; you should abandon this practice, O Illustrious Name.
In seeking wealth, having few desires is supreme, as the Teacher of Gods and Men has extensively proclaimed.
If one can cultivate fewness of desire, though poor, one is truly wealthy.
If a person extensively pursues various matters, they will in turn be afflicted by that much suffering;
if a wise person does not cultivate few desires, they will undergo affliction just like a multi-headed serpent.
By nature resentful like a murderer, She treats her husband with contempt as if he were a mere paramour;
Even for a trifling object, she will surely commit theft— One ought to cast away such a woman who possesses these three vices.

Obedient as a sister, compassionate as a mother, Following like a servant and devoted like a close companion— Such four wives are worthy of support; Know that such a household is called a "home of devas."
Receiving food as if taking medicine, know the proper measure and abandon greed and anger;
do not eat for the sake of fattening or arrogance, but only to sustain the body.
Diligently exerting oneself throughout the long day, during the first and last watches of the night,
Maintain mindfulness even in sleep and dreams; do not let your life end in vain.
Cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; practice these constantly.
Though you have not yet entered the higher realms, you will be able to be reborn in the Brahma world.
Abandoning the mixed desires, suffering, and discursive thoughts, one experiences joy and bliss; according to one's karma, one shall be born among the four stages:
the Great Brahmā, Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, and Bṛhatphala heavens, where one shares the same birth as those beings.
If one constantly cultivates the remedies, One’s virtues will excel and one will compassionately pity sentient beings.
These five practices are good; To fail to practice them is a great evil.
Is salt poured onto a small amount of water Ever like pouring it into a river or a lake?
One should know that even a slight karmic offense can be utterly extinguished by great goodness.
Anger, restlessness, regret, lethargy-and-drowsiness, sensual desire, and doubt—
these five hindrances are like thieves who constantly steal away all wholesome benefits.
There are five most excellent qualities—faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—which one should diligently practice;
they can bring forth the summit of the faculties and powers.
Sickness, suffering, death, and separation from loved ones—all these are caused by one's own karma.
Before you have crossed over, you should practice with diligence; abandon pride and indulgence toward those who are your counterparts.
If you hope for rebirth in heaven or liberation, you must cultivate right view.
Even if a person performs deeds of goodness, wrong view will bring about evil results.
Impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure— those who know this clearly,
Yet harbor deluded thoughts and the four inverted views, find suffering and hardship within this very body.
It is taught that form is not the self, and that the self does not exist within form.
Form is not the self, nor does it exist apart from it; know that the remaining four aggregates are empty.
They do not arise from time, nor are they an inherent nature;
they are not causeless or produced by a sovereign lord, but arise from ignorance, karma, and craving.
The view of precepts and observances, the view of a self, and vicikitsā—know that these three fetters are able to bind the gate of liberation.
Liberation ultimately depends upon oneself; it is not accomplished through the assistance of others.
Diligently cultivate learning, precepts, and concentration, and the Four Noble Truths will arise.
Cultivate the higher training in virtue, mind, and wisdom; this study should be practiced constantly.
The more than one hundred and fifty precepts are all subsumed within these three.
Abide in mindfulness of the body; cultivate this path constantly.
If one allows right mindfulness to decline, all dharmas will utterly perish.
Life is fraught with many calamities, like bubbles blown by the wind.
If one could obtain even a moment’s rest, rising from bed would be a rare occurrence.
In the end, one returns to ash, dryness, and decay; as foul filth, it cannot be maintained for long.
Contemplate that the body is not a substantial reality; it perishes, disintegrates, and falls apart.
When the great earth, Mount Meru, and the oceans are consumed by the flames of seven suns,
how could this most minute body not be reduced to ashes?
Thus impermanent and not lasting long, it has no refuge, no protector, and no home.
Those who excel over birth and death must feel revulsion toward them; they are like the plantain tree, having no core substance.
As rare as a sea turtle encountering the hole of a floating log, a single assembly is extremely difficult to encounter.
Having cast off the body of an animal to become a human body, one still invites the fruits of evil conduct.
To use a precious golden vessel to remove filth is the height of folly;
if one born as a human commits evil deeds, they are truly nothing but the most ignorant of children.
Within this life, rely upon virtuous friends and give rise to right aspirations.
Having previously performed meritorious deeds, one fully attains the four great wheels.
The Buddha said that associating with virtuous friends is the complete holy life;
because the noble ones rely upon the Buddha, many have realized parinirvāṇa.
Through wrong views one is born as a ghost or an animal; in the hells, the Dharma is not heard.
In border regions one becomes a mleccha, or is born with the nature of being dull-witted or mute;
or one is born in the long-lived heavens—having removed these eight states of no leisure, [one finds them].
Now that you have obtained this leisure, you should strive for what is truly meaningful.
Separation from those one loves, old age, sickness, and death—these are the abodes of manifold suffering;
the wise should cultivate weariness toward them, and listen to even a brief account of their faults.
A mother may become a wife, and a father turns into a son;
enemies are transformed into friends—migration flows on without fixed rule.
Each has drunk more mother’s milk than there is water in the four oceans.
Having transmigrated through the bodies of ordinary beings, one has drunk even more [milk] than that.
The bones from each successive birth throughout the past, accumulated one after another, would equal Mount Sumeru;
if the earth were rolled into pellets the size of jujube pits, how could one ever reach the end of counting one’s own physical forms?
Even the Lord of Brahmā, honored by all the world, through the power of karma will ultimately sink to the earth;
though he may succeed as a Wheel-Turning King, his body may be turned over to become a slave or servant.
Having long enjoyed the pleasures of the maidens in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, he shall fall into the hells.
Swiftly and cruelly they pass through various sufferings, their bodies ground and their limbs shattered as they wail incessantly.
On the peaks of Mount Sumeru they experience pleasure, where the earth is soft and yields to their feet;
yet they soon undergo the agony of the Hot Ashes Hell, walking through the prison of Excrement.
In the Fragrant Garden of Joy, celestial maidens roam and play;
yet when they fall into the Forest of Swords, their hands, feet, ears, and noses are severed.
Or they enter the wondrous Mandārava Pool to bathe, where celestial maidens with golden flowers possess radiant and beautiful countenances.
Having abandoned this body, one undergoes further suffering in the hells, where the fierce flames are difficult to endure amidst the ash-rivers.
Even those in the heavens of desire who enjoy the bliss of the Dharma, and even the Great Brahmā gods who have eliminated greed,
may fall again into the Avīci hell, where the agony of firewood and flames is constant and unceasing.
Some are born to dwell among the sun and moon, their bodily radiance pervading the four continents;
yet in a single day they return to the darkness, where even stretching out one's hand provides no means of seeing.
Of the three kinds of lamp-light merit, only this can be carried with one after death.
Entering alone into boundless darkness, where the sun and moon shed no light;
with the Black Rope, the Heat, the Collective Wailing, and the Avīci hells below—
these beings are perpetually entangled in suffering, burning those who have committed evil deeds.
Some are crushed like hemp on a bed, others ground into fine powder;
as if hewn by a sharp axe or split by a saw,
they are constantly boiled in fierce fires and forced to drink hot molten copper.
Driven upward, they are impaled upon swords; their bodies are thrust onto beds of glowing red iron.
At times, with hands raised high, they are devoured by fierce dogs with iron teeth;
hawks and birds with sharp beaks and talons seize them at will to peck at their hearts and livers.
Gnats, flies, and various insects, numbering more than a thousand billion, with their sharp beaks pierce the body; falling in haste, they all devour it.
If a person has committed many sinful deeds, even upon hearing of such suffering, their own body does not tremble or fall [in fear].
Such is this stubborn and deluded vajra-nature; when the breath ceases, one encounters fierce fires in the hells.

At times observing the exhaustion of all transformations, hearing and responding to what is thought, and constantly seeking out the study of sūtras and śāstras—yet having already been struck with terror by the sounds heard in the hells, how can one possibly escape such karmic retribution?
Among all forms of happiness, which is supreme?
The bliss of the exhaustion of craving and the non-arising of suffering is the most refined.
Among all forms of suffering, which is the ultimate?
The suffering of the Avīci Hell is utterly extreme;
compared to the light suffering of being repeatedly pierced by three hundred spears within a single day among humans,
how could they possibly be even a hair’s breadth comparable?
In this place one undergoes extreme suffering for hundreds of koṭis of autumns;
as long as that evil is not exhausted, there is no way to escape death.
Such fruits of various evils are sown by means of body, speech, and mind.
Therefore, you must diligently protect [them] according to your strength; let not even a speck of dust of evil invade them.
Should they enter the realm of animals, they will be constantly beset by the suffering of slaughter and bondage, far removed from the goodness of tranquility, and mutually afflicted by hardships.

Some are subjected to the suffering of being killed or bound; for their pearls, tails, horns, or hides, they are pierced with awls, whipped, hooked, and goaded on the crown of their heads; they are trampled, beaten, and made to carry others.
Their hopes as hungry ghosts remain unfulfilled, and the suffering of having no rival ever descends upon them.
Hunger, thirst, cold, and heat, along with exhaustion, fear, and suffering, constantly assail them.
Their mouths are as small as the eye of a needle, while their bellies are as vast as mountain peaks;
though tormented by hunger, they may even consume their own excrement, yet they find no means to obtain even a little food.
His form is like a withered stump; his skin serves as his clothing.
His mouth burns like a torch night after night, and moths fall into it to serve as food.
Amidst blood, pus, and all manner of impurities, he receives little merit and finds no refuge.
They further revile and press one another with their mouths, only to consume their own swollen goiters and ripe abscesses.
Under the moon they immediately encounter fever; at midday their bodies grow cold.
They look for fruit and find only empty trees; they gaze upon the river and see it has run dry.
Thus one undergoes manifold sufferings for fifteen thousand years;
for such a long time, body and life are struck down, precisely because the vessel of suffering is so solid.
If one is born among the hungry ghosts (preta), one encounters this singular flavor of suffering.
The wise do not cherish that which is coarse; the Buddha taught that it arises from the defilement of stinginess.
Though one experiences pleasure when born in heaven, when merit is exhausted, the suffering is inconceivable.
Since one must ultimately fall back down, know that you should not delight in such things.
The seat is loathed and the robes are stained with grime; the radiance of the body undergoes decay;
fresh sweat flows from beneath the armpits; and the flowers upon the head wither.
When these five signs appear, there is no doubt that the celestial host is dying.
When a person dwelling on earth dies, they become bewildered and lose their usual composure.
If they fall from a celestial realm, all their virtues are exhausted without remainder;
they may then be cast among the animals or hungry ghosts, or fall into one of the hells as they dwell.
The very nature of the asuras, even if they possess complete awakening and wisdom,
leads them to experience the suffering of anger toward the devas and causes them to turn away from the vision of the Truths.
Thus do they drift through the realms of birth and death— the worlds of devas, humans, animals, and asuras.
Born into lowly and base occupations, one becomes a vessel for manifold sufferings; one is cast into the realm of hungry ghosts and even into the hells (*naraka*).

Even if a blazing fire were to burn upon one’s head, with flames pervading all the garments on one’s body, there would be no leisure to brush away this suffering, nor any thought of arising or abiding within *nirvāṇa*.
You seek ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom; Tranquil, disciplined, and supple, free from defilement and calamity.
Nirvana is inexhaustible, without aging or death; The four elements, the sun, and the moon all cease to be.
Mindfulness, the investigation of phenomena, energy, concentration, wisdom, joy, and pliancy—these seven factors of enlightenment can bring about sublime nirvana.
Without wisdom there is no concentration; lacking concentration and wisdom, one sinks into the mire.
If one practices the union of both, the ocean [of suffering] becomes like a cow’s footprint.
Regarding the fourteen indeterminate points taught by the Kinsman of the Sun, one should not dwell upon them; they cannot cause the cessation of awakening.
From ignorance arises karma; from karma, consciousness is born again.
Consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form gives rise to the six sense bases.
The six sense bases condition contact; contact gives rise to feeling.
Feeling has craving as its condition; from craving, grasping is summoned;
grasping, in turn, has becoming as its condition; becoming has birth as its condition;
and birth conditions aging and death, sorrow, affliction, and the failure to obtain what one seeks.
This great mass of suffering in saṃsāra should be swiftly severed;
Just as it arises, so too is it extinguished, And all sufferings will vanish without remainder.
The treasury of the most excellent teachings, The profound and subtle gateway of dependent origination—
If one can see this correctly, one then beholds the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Right view, right intention, right mindfulness, right concentration, right speech, right action, and right thought—
these are called the Eightfold Noble Path, which should be cultivated for the sake of tranquility.
Without cause, craving arises; dependent on the body, manifold sufferings are born.
To eliminate these and realize liberation, one should practice the Noble Eightfold Path.
This very yoga-practice is the cause for the four noble truths.
Though dwelling in a finely adorned house, wisdom blocks the fords of affliction;
one does not fall from the state of emptiness, just as grain is produced because of the earth.
All those who have previously realized the Dharma were once ordinary beings possessed of afflictions.
What need is there for further elaboration? To remove affliction, I present these words in brief:
the matter can be subdued through one's own resolve; the Sage taught that the mind is the source.
Regarding the dharmas thus set forth, it is difficult for a bhikṣu to practice them all in their entirety.
Cultivate even one practice as you are able; do not let your life pass in vain.
Rejoice in all virtues, cultivate the three sublime practices yourself, and dedicate them toward attaining Buddhahood, so that the accumulation of merit may be gathered constantly.
In future lives, his lifespan shall be immeasurable, as he extensively delivers gods and humans;
like Avalokiteśvara, he regards enemies and kin with equal compassion.
Having eliminated birth, old age, sickness, death, and the three poisons, he takes birth in a Buddha-land as the Father of the World.
The span of his life is so long its measure is unknowable, equaling that of the Greatly Awakened Lord Amitābha.
Having revealed and manifested ethical discipline, renunciation, and wisdom, his fame shall spread throughout the earth, the heavens, and the void.
May the inhabitants of the great earth and the hosts of devas never again be wounded by the allure of seductive women.
Sentient beings are bound and entangled by afflictions; Cutting off the flow of birth and death, they ascend to perfect enlightenment.
Transcending the world leaves behind nothing but a name, For by attaining non-arising, one is freed from the turbidity of defilements.
*Ārya-nāga-ṛṣabha-bodhisattva-suhṛd-lekha*. "Ārya" means noble; "nāga" means dragon or elephant;
"ṛṣabha" is translated as "valiant"; "bodhisattva" refers to one whose mind is awakened; "suhṛd" means intimate friend; and "lekha" means a letter.
The previous mention of "Longshu" (Nāgārjuna) was an error.
*Verses of Exhortation by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna to the King*.
